query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C are controlled by the X-element’s ability to modify cation diffusion kinetics and oxide phase stability at the metal/oxide interface. In single-phase solid solutions, minor additions of elements like Al promote the continuous formation of protective Al2O3 (or mixed Cr2O3/Al2O3) layers by reducing the outward diffusion of deleterious cations and enhancing interfacial adhesion, whereas additions such as Mn—with its high mobility— or the presence of multiphase microstructures, promote localized segregation and differential diffusion, leading to discontinuous, stress-prone oxide scales that crack or spall under high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy prepared either as a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solution, with controlled X-element (Si, Mn, or Al) additions, and a baseline composition lacking the minor X-element.
generation.intervention: Systematically alloy CrFeCoNi with a controlled minor addition of X (either Si, Mn, or Al) and process the material to achieve either a single-phase or a deliberately multiphase microstructure, then expose all variants and the baseline alloy (without X) to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures above 900 °C in an oxygen-rich or corrosive environment for prolonged durations sufficient for oxide scale evolution; comparisons made between single-phase and multiphase states at identical temperature and environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural state (single-phase versus multiphase) that modulates local cation diffusion paths and hence the continuity and adhesion of the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The X-element addition modulates the diffusion kinetics of key cations (e.g., Cr, Al, Mn) and governs the formation, phase composition, and interfacial adherence of the emergent oxide scale. In the case of Al addition in a single-phase alloy, reduced cation mobility leads to the gradual buildup of a coherent, protective Al2O3 (and/or mixed Cr2O3-Al2O3) layer. Conversely, in multiphase alloys or when Mn is added, enhanced cation segregation and faster diffusion result in unstable oxide scales that are prone to stress accumulation, cracking, and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al additions in a single-phase state will form a continuous, slowly growing, and adherent oxide scale (dominated by Al2O3 and possibly Cr2O3), whereas alloys with Mn additions or those with multiphase microstructures will display non-uniform oxide layers that crack or spall due to uneven diffusion and adhesion issues.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloy without any X-element addition, expected to form less coherent oxide scales (e.g., predominantly chromia with mixed oxides) that are more prone to spallation under high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Applicable to high-temperature oxidation conditions above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and within the compositional/microstructural regimes of single-phase and multiphase CrFeCoNi-based alloys.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the reduction in cation diffusivity and the stress accommodation improvement imparted by the X-element additions, as well as the transition thresholds between coherent and spalled oxide regimes under varying environmental parameters, remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNi alloys with controlled additions of Si, Mn, and Al in both single-phase and multiphase microstructures alongside a baseline alloy without X. Expose each sample to a sustained high-temperature oxidative atmosphere (e.g., 950–1050 °C in air or a defined corrosive gas mixture) for equivalent durations. Characterize the oxide scale morphology, composition, and adhesion using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and possibly focused ion beam (FIB) cross-sectioning to measure oxide continuity and interface integrity.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (via XRD/EDS)
Oxide scale continuity and adherence (via SEM and cross-sectional imaging)
Cation diffusion profiles near the oxide/metal interface (using techniques such as SIMS or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Al-added and single-phase samples do not exhibit significantly improved oxide adherence or coherent protective scale formation—compared to the baseline and to Mn-added or multiphase samples—or if there is no observable difference in cation diffusion rates and oxide phase stability between the experimental and baseline groups under the defined conditions, then the proposed mechanism is refuted.

Alloys used in extreme environments, such as turbines and aero-engines, require excellent high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance. Recent progress in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which have five or more elements present in near-equimolar proportions, has resulted in several alloys with excellent high-temperature strength. However, the oxidation and corrosion behavior of HEAs is still poorly understood and modeled. Oxidation is an extremely complex process where kinetics, thermodynamics, and microstructure play a competing role in forming the passivating oxide layer, which prevents a catastrophic oxidation [,]. Challenges in modeling the oxidation behavior of HEAs are numerous, including understanding the role of chemistry, microstructure, grain boundaries, associated volume changes, stresses in the oxide scale, and the environment itself, along with the thermodynamic stabilities at elevated temperature and the kinetics of the process. frame.system: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
frame.goal: To establish a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains why, under high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive conditions, some alloy compositions form a stable, coherent protective oxide layer while others develop unstable, cracking/spalling oxides.
frame.limitation: An incomplete mechanistic understanding of which compositional or microstructural factors control the adhesion, integrity, and persistence of the oxide scale during prolonged high-temperature exposure.

unstable surface oxides that crack or spall

constraints: The hypothesis must specify the governing mechanism (e.g., oxide scale composition, elemental diffusion, and phase stability) that leads to either stable or unstable oxide formation.
A controlled comparison against a defined baseline is required (for example, comparing the effects of X-element additions vs. a baseline alloy without the X-element).
The hypothesis should clearly predict the differences in oxide behaviour between single- and multiphase states, and account for the specific influence of Si, Mn, or Al additions.
Applicable boundaries include high-temperature exposure (above 900 °C) and the operational conditions of an oxidative/corrosive atmosphere.
frame.regime: Exposure in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures exceeding 900 °C, with the alloy material presented either as a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solution.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have explored compositional variations in high-entropy alloys to form protective oxides, but these approaches often lacked a unified mechanistic framework linking microstructure and elemental diffusion kinetics with oxide adhesion. This left ambiguity regarding why certain compositions fail (leading to cracking and spallation) and others succeed.

decision.trend: Early oxidation studies in high‐entropy alloys first documented that at high temperature (near or above 900 °C) the oxide scales could either adhere or spall – with experiments on alloys such as Cr‐Mn‐Fe‐Co systems showing parabolic oxidation kinetics and eventual cracking of the oxide layer. Successive work then applied controlled processing (e.g., rapid thermal spraying, annealing, and in‐situ techniques) and advanced characterization (atom probe, TEM, XANES) to dissect how elemental diffusion and oxide phase evolution contribute to the formation and failure of protective layers. However, while these studies identified factors such as redox potential differences, cation mobility, and microstructural state (single‐ versus multiphase) as key players, a unified mechanistic framework that precisely connects minor alloying additions (here, Si, Mn, or Al) with the evolution of a coherent, stable oxide scale remains lacking.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved how the incorporation of a minor X-element (Si, Mn, or Al) modulates the cation diffusion kinetics, oxide scale phase stability, and interfacial adhesion in a controlled baseline comparison, especially when contrasting single-phase versus multiphase solid solutions. The specific interplay between controlled elemental additions, oxide chemistry, and interfacial energy barriers governing stable versus unstable oxide formation at temperatures above 900 °C has yet to be conclusively established.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the X-element addition (Si, Mn, or Al) in CrFeCoNi alloys while controlling for single- versus multiphase microstructures to quantify how these additions affect cation diffusion rates, oxide scale composition, and interfacial adhesion under high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative/corrosive exposure.
decision.why: This approach directly builds upon the trend of progressively linking compositional modifications to oxidation behavior. By comparing baseline CrFeCoNi with each X-added variant under identical conditions, researchers can isolate the role of the X-element in modifying diffusion kinetics and phase stability at the oxide/metal interface, addressing the gap concerning why and how protective oxide scales persist in some cases while spall in others.
